title: The Dinner
blurb: It's Gran's birthday and the family come for dinner at seven — but Gran is ill upstairs, and tonight the cooking is all yours. With a takeaway man offering an easy cheat and the clock running down, you have two hours to get a good evening onto the table, and to decide who you let through the door.

identity.name: Dinner at Seven
identity.mood: A warm kitchen on a winter evening; dinner for the people you love, and two hours to get it right.

cover.alt: A warm, lit kitchen window on a dark winter street at night: steam on the glass, a pot on the hob and a table laid for dinner inside.

line.en: The family come for dinner at seven, and tonight the cooking is all yours. Get a good evening onto the table.
line.fr: La famille vient dîner à sept heures, et ce soir, c'est toi qui cuisines. Prépare une belle soirée à table.
line.es: La familia viene a cenar a las siete, y esta noche cocinas tú. Pon una buena velada en la mesa.
line.it: La famiglia viene a cena alle sette, e stasera cucini tu. Porta in tavola una bella serata.
line.de: Die Familie kommt um sieben zum Essen, und heute Abend kochst du. Bring einen schönen Abend auf den Tisch.
line.pt: A família vem jantar às sete, e esta noite quem cozinha és tu. Põe uma boa noite na mesa.
line.ru: Семья придёт на ужин в семь, и сегодня готовишь ты. Накрой хороший вечер на стол.
line.zh: 家人七点来吃晚饭，今晚做饭全靠你了。为大家张罗一桌好饭、一个好夜晚。
line.ar: تأتي العائلة للعشاء في السابعة، والليلة الطبخ كله عليك. قدِّم أمسية جميلة على المائدة.

text.A2: You call your mum to ask what to do. The phone rings and rings. At last she answers. She can't come over tonight, she says. She is too far away. But she talks you through Gran's recipe, step by step. 'You can do this,' she says.

text.A2: You stop and think. You could start cooking right now. You could go up to Gran and the family first. Or you could call friends to come and help. Each choice costs time you do not have. And the clock keeps moving toward seven.

text.A2: You can't stop now. But you can't just leave them, either. So you promise to send help round soon. 'Hang on,' you say. 'Stay warm, stay put — I won't forget you.' You mean it, too. And then you go.
text.B1: You can't stop now — but you can't just leave them, either. So you promise to send help round soon. 'Hang on,' you say. 'Stay warm, stay put — I won't forget you.' You mean it, too. And then you turn and go.
text.B2: You can't stop now — but you can't simply leave them, either. So you promise to send help round soon. 'Hang on,' you say, over the rain. 'Stay warm, stay put — I won't forget you.' You mean it, too; and then you turn and go, carrying the weight of it with you.

text.A2: You and the friends get one big pot going — a warm stew that will feed everyone. People gather round the warm hob. It is not the whole dinner. But it is real food, and a start.
text.B1: You and the friends get one big pot going — a warm stew that will feed everyone, whatever else happens. People gather round the warm hob. It isn't the whole dinner. But it's real food, and a good beginning.
text.B2: You and the friends get one big pot going — a warm, simple stew that will feed everyone, whatever else happens with the clock. People gather round the warm hob, glad of it. It isn't the whole dinner, not by a long way. But it's real food, and a good beginning, and the kitchen smells of it.

text.A2: Friend by friend, the panic turns into a working kitchen. People have jobs now: one peels, one stirs, one lays the table. Worry turns into doing. And doing beats worrying, every single time. The kitchen fills up with noise and warmth.
text.B1: Friend by friend, the panic turns into a working kitchen. People have jobs now: one peels, one stirs, one lays the table. Worry turns into doing. And doing beats worrying, every single time. The kitchen fills up with noise and warmth.
text.B2: Friend by friend, task by task, the panic turns into a working kitchen. People have jobs now: one peels the potatoes, one stirs a pot, one lays the table under your eye. Worry turns into doing — and doing beats worrying, in a kitchen, every single time. The kitchen fills up with noise and warmth, and the worst of the panic lifts.

text.A2: To the shop for the rest.
text.B1: To the shop for the rest.
text.B2: To the shop for the rest.

text.A2: The long evening wears at you. A voice says: give up, order a takeaway, put your feet up. No one would blame you, and it would be easy. But you think of Gran's face at a full table. And you push the voice away. Not yet.
text.B1: The long evening wears at you. A small voice says: give up, order a takeaway, put your feet up — no one would blame you, and it would be so easy. But you think of Gran's face at a full table. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while it can still be good.
text.B2: The long evening wears at you. A small voice says: give up, order a takeaway, put your feet up — no one would blame you, and it would be so easy to do. But you think of Gran's face coming down to a full, warm table. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while the evening can still be good.

text.A2: You stop under a lamp to read the rest of Gran's list. Half of it is smudged by the rain. You could push on to the shop for the rest. Or something makes you look back at the gate, and that soft knock.
text.B1: You stop under a street lamp to read the rest of Gran's list. Half of it is smudged by the rain. You could push on to the shop and get the rest. Or something makes you look back at the gate, and that soft knock you heard.
text.B2: You stop under a street lamp to read the rest of Gran's list, but half of it is smudged and run by the rain. You could push on to the shop and get the last few things. Or something makes you look back, down the dark street, toward the gate and that soft knock you heard earlier.

text.A2: Dale leans in close, all friendly. 'Cold out here,' he says. 'I've got the lot — chicken, spuds, all hot. Tip it in your dishes, no one knows. Why make trouble for yourself?' His smile is wide. But his eyes don't smile with it.
text.B1: Dale leans in close, all friendly. 'Cold out here,' he says. 'I've got the lot — chicken, spuds, all hot and ready. Tip it into your dishes, and no one's any the wiser. Why make all this trouble for yourself?' His smile is wide. But his eyes don't smile with it.
text.B2: Dale leans in close, all friendly. 'Cold out here,' he says. 'I've got the lot — chicken, spuds, all hot and ready to go. Tip it into your own dishes, and no one's ever any the wiser. Why make all this trouble for yourself, love?' His smile is wide and easy. But his eyes don't smile along with it, and you notice that.

text.A2: 'Fair price,' Dale says, and names a sum that makes you blink. It's a lot. But he's quick, he's hot, and he's right here. No shop, no cooking, no mess. So: pay him, turn him down, or ask him straight what his game is?
text.B1: 'Fair price,' Dale says, and names a sum that makes you blink. It's a lot of money. But he's quick, he's hot, and he's right here in front of you. No shop, no cooking, no mess to clear up. So what's it to be — pay him, turn him down, or ask what his game is?
text.B2: 'Fair price,' Dale says, and names a sum that makes you blink in the rain. It's a lot of money, more than the shop would ever charge. But he's quick, he's hot, and he's right here in front of you now. No shop, no cooking, no mess to clear up after. So what's it to be — pay him, turn him down flat, or ask him straight out what his game really is?

text.A2: You say no thanks and walk on. It feels good to turn him down. He calls after you, but you don't look back. His sort always find someone. But it won't be you, not tonight.
text.B1: You say no thanks and walk on past him. It feels good to turn him down. He calls something after you, but you don't look back. His sort always find someone, in the end. But it won't be you, not tonight.
text.B2: You say no thanks and walk on past him into the rain. It feels good to turn him down flat. He calls something after you, but you don't look back. His sort always find someone, in the end — someone tired and frightened enough. But it won't be you, not tonight.

text.A2: You take his food and hand over the money. Your hands close on the warm bags, and part of you already knows. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart. It feels like a small lie starting.
text.B1: You take his food and hand over the money. Your hands close on the warm bags, and part of you already knows. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart at all. It feels like a small lie, just starting.
text.B2: You take his food and hand over the money. Your hands close on the warm bags, and part of you already knows the truth of it. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart at all. It feels, in the cold, like a small lie being told — one you'll have to keep telling all evening.

text.A2: You ask him straight: why so keen to help? He laughs. 'Easy money, love,' he says. 'A flop tonight, and you'll be back to mine next week.' He's honest, at least. That tells you all you need to know.
text.B1: You ask him straight: why is he so keen to help? He laughs. 'Easy money, love,' he says. 'A flop tonight, and you'll be back to mine next week.' He laughs again. At least he's honest — and that tells you all you need to know.
text.B2: You ask him straight out: why is he so keen to help? He laughs, quite openly. 'Easy money, love,' he says. 'And if your dinner's a flop tonight, you'll be back to mine next week, won't you.' At least he's honest about it — and that, right there, tells you everything you need to know.

text.A2: You tip his food into your own dishes. But up close it looks wrong — greasy, grey, nothing like Gran's. It won't fool anyone at the table. The whole thing already feels like a mistake.
text.B1: You tip his food into your own dishes. But up close it looks all wrong — greasy, grey, nothing like Gran's cooking. It won't fool anyone at the table for a second. The whole thing already feels like a mistake.
text.B2: You tip his food into your own dishes and try to make it look like yours. But up close it looks all wrong — greasy, grey, and nothing at all like Gran's cooking. It won't fool anyone at that table for a second. And the whole thing already feels, in your stomach, like a mistake.

text.A2: You open the bag, and the smell hits you — cold grease, old fat, nothing fresh. This food won't pass for home cooking. You paid good money, and it's not worth it. The bad feeling in your gut was right.
text.B1: You open the bag, and the smell hits you — cold grease, old fat, nothing fresh about it. This food will never pass for home cooking. You paid good money for it, and it's not worth it. The bad feeling in your gut was right all along.
text.B2: You open the bag, and the smell hits you — cold grease, old fat, nothing fresh about any of it. This food will never pass for home cooking, not at Gran's table. You paid good money for it, out here in the rain, and it's not worth it. The bad feeling in your gut was right about him all along.

text.A2: You turn to find Dale, but he's already gone, off into the rain. He was never really helping. He just wanted the sale, and a flop tonight so you'd come back. You've been had, plain and simple.
text.B1: You turn to find Dale, but he's already gone, off into the rain. He was never really helping you. He just wanted the sale — and a flop tonight, so you'd come back to him. You've been had, plain and simple.
text.B2: You turn to find Dale, but he's already gone, melted off into the rain. He was never really helping you at all. He just wanted the sale — and a flop tonight, so you'd be back at his counter next week. You've been had, out here, plain and simple. The rain keeps on, and the money's gone with him.

text.A2: He's gone, and the street is empty. Just the rain now, and the money you gave him for nothing. You learned something tonight. And you paid too much for it. Now you go on with less than you had.
text.B1: He's gone, and the street is empty — just the rain now, and the money you handed him for nothing. You learned something tonight. And you paid far too much for it. Now you go on with less than you started with.
text.B2: He's gone, and the street is empty — just the rain now, the dark, and the money you handed him for nothing at all. You learned something tonight, out here. And you paid far too much for it. Now you go on with less than you started with, and the clock no kinder.

text.A2: Stand a moment in the rain.
text.B1: Stand a moment in the rain.
text.B2: Stand a moment in the rain.

text.A2: Other tired people are buying from Dale too, hands full of money, glad of the easy way. He takes it slow, with that same smile. He only helps the ones who pay the most.
text.B1: Other tired people are buying from Dale too — hands full of money, glad of the easy way out. He takes it slow, with that same smile. He only ever helps the ones who can pay the most.
text.B2: Other tired people are buying from Dale too — hands full of money, glad of any easy way out tonight. He takes it slow, unhurried, with that same wide smile. He only ever helps the ones who can pay him the most — and you see the whole of him in it.

text.A2: You're halfway across the main road now. The far side looks close — or does it? The rain and the headlights play tricks. And you are a long way from both kerbs.
text.B1: You're halfway across the main road now. The far side looks close — or does it? The rain and the headlights play tricks on your eyes. And you're a long way from both kerbs, out in the middle.
text.B2: You're halfway across the main road now, and the far side looks close — or does it? The rain and the swinging headlights play tricks on your tired eyes. And you're a long way from both kerbs, out in the middle of it, with the traffic coming. You keep your feet moving, and you do not look down.

text.A2: A car comes fast out of the dark, its lights filling your eyes. This is the moment. You can keep going and hope it stops. Or you can jump back to the kerb, while you still can.
text.B1: A car comes fast out of the dark, its lights filling your eyes, its horn blaring. This is the moment. You can keep going and hope it stops in time. Or you can jump back to the kerb, while you still can.
text.B2: A car comes fast out of the dark, its lights filling your eyes, its horn blaring over the rain. This is the moment, and it's a short one. You can keep going and hope it stops in time. Or you can throw yourself back toward the kerb, right now, while you still can.

text.A2: You reach the far side at last, soaked and shaking — but across. Somehow you made it. Now you must choose. Push on, shaken as you are? Or go back for what you dropped in the road?
text.B1: You reach the far side at last, soaked and shaking, your heart going hard — but across. Somehow you made it. Now you have to decide: push on, shaken as you are, or go back for what you dropped in the road.
text.B2: You reach the far side at last, soaked and shaking, your heart going hard against your ribs — but across. Somehow, against the odds, you made it. Now you have to decide: push on, shaken as you are, or go back for the shopping you dropped out there in the road.

text.A2: You jump back to the kerb just in time — the right, hard choice. The car roars past, close enough to feel. You stand there shaking, but safe. The night isn't lost. But you've lost time, and you'll go round now.
text.B1: You jump back to the kerb just in time — the hard, right choice. The car roars past, close enough to feel the wind of it. You stand there shaking, but safe. The night isn't lost. But you've lost time you'll miss — and you'll go the long way now.
text.B2: You throw yourself back to the kerb just in time — the hard choice, and the right one. The car roars past, close enough to feel the wind of it on your face. You stand there shaking, but safe. The night isn't lost. But you've lost time you'll badly miss — and you'll go the long way round now, like you should have.

text.A2: You try to help with their dinner. Put a pan on, find what's in the cupboard, get something warm going. It helps a little. But they've next to nothing in, and you can't stay long. There's only one real thing you can do.
text.B1: You try to help with their dinner — put a pan on, see what's in the cupboard, get something warm started. It helps a little. But they've next to nothing in the house, and you can't stay long. There's really only one thing you can do for them.
text.B2: You try to help with their dinner — put a pan on, see what's in the near-empty cupboard, get something warm started for the kids. It helps a little. But they've next to nothing in the house, and you can't stay long tonight. There's really only one thing left that you can do for them.

text.A2: You hand over your own bags of food, and the family's faces change. The kids crowd round the table. The little one stops crying. 'Thank you,' the mum says — then she tells you someone's waiting at your gate.
text.B1: You hand over your own bags of food, and the family's faces change. The kids crowd round the table at the thought of a hot meal. The little one stops crying at last. 'Thank you,' the mum says — and then she tells you someone's been waiting at your gate.
text.B2: You hand over your own bags of food, and the family's tired faces change all at once. The kids crowd round the table at the thought of a hot meal. The little one stops crying at last. 'Thank you,' the mum says, over and over — and then she tells you someone's been waiting at your gate, in the rain.

text.A2: With your own food given away, your heart sinks a little. Now there's less for your own table. You gave it to help, and you'd do it again. But the clock doesn't care about that. It just keeps ticking.
text.B1: With your own food given away, your heart sinks a little. Now there's less for your own table at seven. You gave it to help, and you'd do it again. But the clock doesn't care about any of that. It just keeps ticking on.
text.B2: With your own food given away, your heart sinks a little in your chest. Now there's that much less for your own table at seven. You gave it away to help, and you'd do it again in a heartbeat. But the clock on the wall doesn't care about any of that. It just keeps ticking on toward the hour.

text.A2: A warm café offers a sit-down.
text.B1: A warm café offers a sit-down.
text.B2: A warm café offers a sit-down.

text.A2: A neighbour waves you into a warm café. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, dry off, have a cuppa.' It's warm in there. Your tired feet beg you to stop. But five minutes can turn into twenty.
text.B1: A neighbour waves you into a warm café. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, dry off, have a cup of tea.' It's warm and dry inside, and your tired feet beg you to stop. But five minutes like this can quietly turn into twenty.
text.B2: A neighbour waves you into a warm, bright café out of the rain. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, dry off, have a cup of tea.' It's warm and dry in there, and your cold, tired feet beg you to stop. But five minutes like this one can quietly turn into twenty, with the clock running.

text.A2: You press on through the rain, cold and wet. Your bags are heavy, the clock in your head. Each step is a small effort now. But you keep them coming, one after another, toward home and the kitchen.
text.B1: You press on through the rain, cold and wet, your bags heavy, the clock ticking in your head. Each step is a small effort now. But you keep them coming, one after another, toward home and the warm kitchen.
text.B2: You press on through the rain, cold and wet to the skin, your bags heavy in your hands and the clock ticking loud in your head. Each step is a small effort on its own now. But you keep them coming, one after another after another, toward home and the warm, waiting kitchen.

text.A2: A neighbour stops you. 'There's someone down the road,' they say, 'out in the rain, lost. Been there an hour. No coat, no umbrella.' Out there is just the dark and the cold. If no one goes to them, they'll be there all night.
text.B1: A neighbour stops you. 'There's someone down the road,' they say, 'standing out in the rain, lost. Been there an hour. No coat, no umbrella.' Out there is just the dark and the cold. If no one goes to them, they'll be there all night.
text.B2: A neighbour stops you in the street. 'There's someone down the road,' they say, 'standing out in the rain, quite lost. Been there the best part of an hour. No coat, no umbrella, nothing.' Out there is just the dark and the cold. If no one goes to them tonight, they'll be there until morning.

text.A2: You find them down the road, soaked through and shaking, lost. The cold has got right into them. They don't seem to know where they are. You take a firm hold of their arm. 'Come with me,' you say. 'You're all right now. I've got you.'
text.B1: You find them down the road, soaked through and shaking, lost. The cold has got right into them. They don't seem to know quite where they are. You take a firm hold of their arm. 'Come with me,' you say. 'You're all right now. I've got you.'
text.B2: You find them down the road, soaked through and shaking, utterly lost. The cold has got right into them. They don't seem to know quite where they are, or who you are. You take a firm hold of their arm. 'Come with me,' you say, over the rain. 'You're all right now. I've got you.'

text.A2: You can't do it all at once, and the dinner needs you most. So you send word for someone else to go to them, and press on home. It sits badly with you. But tonight you have to choose, and keep choosing.
text.B1: You can't do it all at once, and the dinner needs you most of all. So you send word for someone else to go to them, and press on home. It sits badly with you. But tonight you have to choose, and keep on choosing.
text.B2: You can't do it all at once, and the dinner needs you most of all tonight. So you send word for someone else to go to them, and press on home through the rain. It sits badly with you, and will for a while. But tonight you have to choose, and keep on choosing.

text.A2: You walk them safely to a warm doorway, where friends take them in. Their faces fill with relief. They wrap the stranger in a dry coat and sit them down by the fire. 'Thank you,' they keep saying to you. But your own kitchen is waiting, and you can't stay long.
text.B1: You walk them safely to a warm doorway, where friends take them in. Their faces fill with relief. They wrap the stranger in a dry coat and sit them down by the fire. 'Thank you,' they keep saying to you. But your own kitchen is waiting, and you can't stay long tonight.
text.B2: You walk them safely to a warm doorway, where friends take them in at once. Their faces fill with relief at the sight. They wrap the stranger in a dry coat and sit them down by the fire. 'Thank you,' they keep saying to you, over and over. But your own kitchen is waiting across the dark, and you can't stay long.

text.A2: You stop and look down the long wet street. The rain falls through the lamplight, soft and steady. The houses are dark, the curtains drawn, everyone in for the night. Only one small light moves, far off. The whole street seems to hold its breath.
text.B1: You stop and look down the long wet street. The rain falls through the lamplight, soft and steady. The houses are dark, the curtains drawn, everyone in for the night. Only one small light moves, far off down the road. The whole street seems to hold its breath.
text.B2: You stop and look down the long, wet street. The rain falls through the lamplight, soft and steady and endless. The houses are dark, the curtains drawn, everyone in for the night. Only one small light moves, far off down the road, where it has no business being. The whole street seems to hold its breath and wait.

text.A2: The night turns as hard as it gets. The rain comes down in sheets now, and the cold bites through your coat. It's hard to think, hard to move, hard to care. Your bags feel like lead. This is the worst of it.
text.B1: The night turns as hard as it gets now. The rain comes down in sheets, and the cold bites through your coat. It's hard to think, hard to move, hard to care. Your bags feel like lead in your hands. This is the worst of it — the hardest part of the whole evening.
text.B2: The night turns as hard as it is going to get. The rain comes down in sheets now, and the cold bites straight through your coat. It's hard to think, hard to move, hard to care about any of it. Your bags feel like lead in your hands. This is the worst of it — the hardest part of the whole long evening.

text.A2: Old Sam presses a parcel into your hands — the last good cut of meat in the shop. 'For the table,' he says. 'Go on, take it. I'll put it on the tab.' His face is kind under the shop light. It's what he has to give tonight, and he gives it gladly.
text.B1: Old Sam presses a parcel into your hands — the last good cut of meat in the shop. 'For the table,' he says. 'Go on, take it. I'll put it on your tab.' His face is kind under the shop light. It's what he has to give tonight, and he gives all of it gladly.
text.B2: Old Sam presses a wrapped parcel into your hands — the last good cut of meat left in the shop. 'For the table,' he says. 'Go on, take it. I'll put it on your tab.' His face is kind under the shop light. It's what he has to give tonight, and he gives every bit of it gladly.

text.A2: At the shop door, people are grabbing the last of the food. Voices rise, hands push, fear spreading fast. One more shove and it's a fight. You can try to calm them and share it out fairly. Or you can grab what's yours and go.
text.B1: At the shop door, people are grabbing the last of the food. Voices rise, hands push, fear spreading fast through the queue. One more shove and it's a fight. You can try to calm them and share it out fairly. Or you can grab what's yours and go.
text.B2: At the shop door, people are grabbing the last of the food off the shelves. Voices rise, hands push, fear spreading fast through the queue. One more shove and it tips into a fight. You can try to calm them down and share it out fairly. Or you can grab what's yours and go.

text.A2: A dark, quiet corner by the gate, where nothing seems to move. The rain drips. The cold creeps in. Then you hear it — breathing, weak and close, out of the dark. Someone is here after all, huddled down against the wall.
text.B1: A dark, quiet corner by the gate, where nothing seems to move at all. The rain drips. The cold creeps in. Then you hear it — breathing, weak and close, out of the dark. Someone is here after all, huddled down against the wall.
text.B2: A dark, quiet corner by the gate, where nothing seems to move at all. The rain drips from the eaves. The cold creeps in around you. Then you hear it — breathing, weak and close, somewhere out of the dark. Someone is here after all, huddled down against the cold wall.

text.A2: Far down the dark street, a small light lifts and fades. It's out where no one should be, this late, in this rain. Showing, then gone, then showing again. You can't explain it. And something in you wants to go and answer it.
text.B1: Far down the dark street, a small light lifts and fades. It's out where no one should be, this late, in this rain. Showing, then gone, then showing again. No one could explain it. And something in you wants to go and answer it.
text.B2: Far down the dark street, a small light lifts and fades, lifts and fades. It's out where no one should be, this late, in this kind of rain. Showing, then gone, then showing again, patient as anything. No one could explain it. And something in you wants to go and answer it.

text.A2: You go down toward the light and call into the dark. No answer comes but the rain. Then you see it — a small shape, down low against a wall, half-hidden in the dark. Someone is out here after all. And they are barely moving.
text.B1: You go down toward the light and call into the dark. No answer comes back but the rain. Then you see it — a small shape, down low against a wall, half-hidden in the dark. Someone is out here after all. And they are barely moving.
text.B2: You go on down toward the light and call into the dark. No answer comes back but the rain and the wind. Then you see it — a small shape, down low against a wall, half-hidden in the dark. Someone is out here after all, alone. And they are barely moving now.

text.A2: You reach them, and your heart turns over. It's a young woman — Nora — huddled against the wall, soaked and shaking, barely awake. The cold has got right into her. There's no time to stop and think. You have to do something now.
text.B1: You reach them, and your heart turns over. It's a young woman — Nora — huddled against the wall, soaked and shaking, barely awake. The cold has got right into her. There's no time to stop and think about it. You have to do something now.
text.B2: You reach them, and your heart turns right over. It's a young woman — Nora — huddled against the wall, soaked and shaking, barely awake at all. The cold has got right into her now. There's no time to stop and think it through. You have to do something, and do it now.

text.A2: You call again into the dark, and for a moment there's nothing. Then a thin voice comes back, shaking with cold: 'Here! Over here!' Someone is out in the rain, and they need help. And they don't sound strong at all.
text.B1: You call again into the dark, and for a moment there's nothing at all. Then a thin voice comes back, shaking with cold: 'Here! Over here!' Someone is out in the rain, and they need help. And they don't sound strong at all.
text.B2: You call again into the dark, and for a long moment there's nothing at all. Then a thin voice comes back, torn and shaking with cold: 'Here! Over here!' Someone is out in the rain, and they need help badly. And they don't sound strong at all. You cup your hands and shout back into the rain.

text.A2: You get Nora up out of the wet and wrap her tight in your coat. Slowly she comes round, gripping your arm. 'The door,' she whispers. 'Is the door still open...?' Even now, half-frozen, she's thinking of someone's door.
text.B1: You get Nora up out of the wet and wrap her tight in your own coat. Slowly she comes round, gripping your arm. 'The door,' she whispers. 'Is the door still open...?' Even now, half-frozen, she's thinking of someone's door.
text.B2: You get Nora up out of the wet and wrap her tight in your own coat. Slowly she comes round, gripping your arm hard. 'The door,' she whispers. 'Is the door still open...?' Even now, half-frozen in the rain, she's thinking of someone's door. You keep your arm around her, and hold on.

text.A2: You turn to run for help — then stop short. There's no one out here to call, not at this hour. No neighbours up, no one coming. It's you or no one, and she knows it too. Her frightened eyes follow you in the dark.
text.B1: You turn to run for help — then stop short. There's no one out here to call, not at this hour. No neighbours up, no one coming for you. It's you or no one now, and she knows it too. Her frightened eyes follow you in the dark.
text.B2: You turn to run for help — then stop short. There's no one out here to call on, not at this hour of the night. No neighbours up, no one coming for either of you. It's you or no one now, and she knows it too. Her frightened eyes follow you in the dark.

text.A2: Then it's you. Go to her.
text.B1: Then it's you. Go to her.
text.B2: Then it's you. Go to her.

text.A2: Nora looks up at you, her eyes clearer now. 'Ivy's my gran,' she says. 'We haven't spoken in years. Not since my mum and her fell out. It's a long, sad story.' And you hear just how long it is.

text.A2: You decide to get them face to face before the night is out. Nora and old Gran Ivy, after all these years. It's a small thing, next to everything else tonight. But it's not nothing. Some shut doors can still be opened.

But it is not nothing. Some shut doors can still be opened, if someone tries. And tonight, it seems, that someone is you.

text.A2: The small shape isn't moving, and the cold is working on it, slow and patient. And yet someone came all this way out here, in the rain, alone. You can't just leave them lying in the wet. You have to go closer and see who it is.

text.A2: You go closer, and you know her at once. It's Nora — Gran Ivy's own granddaughter, not seen round here in years, not since the family fell out. Then a weak sound comes from the dark at your feet. You move fast now.
text.B1: You go closer, and you know her at once. It's Nora — Gran Ivy's own granddaughter, not seen round here in years, not since the family fell out. Then a weak sound comes from the dark at your feet. You move fast now.
text.B2: You go closer still, and you know her at once. It's Nora — Gran Ivy's own granddaughter, not seen round here in years, not since the family fell out so badly. Then a weak sound comes from the dark at your feet. You move fast now. There is no time left to lose, none at all.

text.A2: Dale turns up one last time, his bags swinging. 'Still at it?' he says. 'Give it up. Let me sort your dinner — last chance to take the easy road, friend.' The same easy smile. The same old lie.
text.B1: Dale turns up one last time, his bags swinging. 'Still at it?' he says. 'Give it up. Let me sort your dinner out — last chance to take the easy road, friend.' The same easy smile. The same old lie.
text.B2: Dale turns up one last time, his bags swinging in the rain. 'Still at it?' he says. 'Give it up, love. Let me sort your dinner out — last chance to take the easy road, friend.' The same easy smile. The same old lie underneath it. You've seen exactly where that road goes.

text.A2: You're home at last, soaked and worn out, with seven almost here. Upstairs, Gran Ivy lies pale and weak in her bed. The kitchen is cold, the oven off, the table bare. This is the moment it all rests on. Everything now comes down to what you do next.

text.A2: You get to the kitchen: the oven cold, nothing on, the clock ticking hard. Out in the rain, the night is still taking people. You have to get the dinner on and the kitchen warm again. And you have to choose what matters most, right now.

text.A2: Then help reaches you at last — more hands, friends at the door, people who know a kitchen. You're not alone with this now. Others are here to share the load. It's like setting down something heavy you carried too far, too long.

text.A2: Now you keep the dinner going. What you can make depends on what you carried home. With a full basket, you've plenty to work with. Without it, you must make every last scrap count. Either way, the work is the same: keep going.

text.A2: You go up to check on Gran Ivy. Her eyes open just a little. There's fear in them — then, seeing your face, a bit less fear. 'You're cooking,' she whispers. 'That I am,' you tell her softly. 'Now you rest.'

text.A2: The full basket does it. You light the oven, fill the pots, and soon the smells rise — meat, gravy, bread. The kitchen glows warm and golden against the dark window. This, you think, is what a home should feel like.
text.B1: The full basket does it. You light the oven, fill the pots, and soon the smells rise — meat, gravy, warm bread. The kitchen glows warm and golden against the dark window. This, you think to yourself, is what a home should feel like.
text.B2: The full basket does the trick. You light the oven, fill the pots, and before long the smells begin to rise — meat, gravy, warm bread, all of it. text.A2: You've not much food to work with, so you stretch every scrap. A little meat, some veg, a lot of care. You make the one pot go as far as it can. It's thin, and plain. It may be enough — or it may not.
text.B1: You've not much food to work with, so you stretch every last scrap. A little meat, some veg, and a lot of care. You make the one pot go as far as it possibly can. It's thin, and plain. It may just be enough — or it may not.
text.B2: You've not much food to work with at all, so you stretch every last scrap as far as it will go. A little meat, some veg, and a great deal of care. You make the one pot go as far as it can possibly stretch. It's thin, and plain, and honest. It may just about be enough to go round — or, then again, it may not.

text.A2: The meal is thin, and you're afraid it won't stretch to everyone. You've done all you can with what you have. But it may still fall short at the table. You need more now — more food, more hands, or both.
text.B1: The meal is thin, and you're afraid it won't stretch to everyone at the table. You've done all you can with what little you have. But it may still fall short in the end. You need more now — more food, more hands, or both.
text.B2: The meal is thin, and you're honestly afraid it won't stretch to everyone at the table tonight. You've done all you possibly can with the little you have. But even so, it may still fall short when they all sit down. You need more now — more food, more hands, or, if you're to manage this, probably both.

text.A2: You glance out the window and see it. Far down the street, a light flares and falls. It shows where no one should be, hiding and showing again. It pulls at your eye. And it pulls at something deeper than that.
text.B1: You glance out the window and see it. Far down the street, a light flares and falls. It shows where no one should be tonight, hiding and showing again. It pulls at your eye. And it pulls at something deeper than that.
text.B2: You glance out of the window and you see it. Far down the dark street, a small light flares and falls. It shows where no one on earth should be tonight, hiding itself and then showing again. It pulls at your eye, that light. And it pulls, if you're honest, at something a good deal deeper than that.

text.A2: The light down the street shows again. It shows where everyone says no one would be. But a light means a hand to hold it. A hand means a person. A person out there, alone, in rain and cold like this.
text.B1: The light down the street shows again. It shows where everyone swears no one would be. But a light means a hand to hold it. A hand means a person. A person out there, alone, in rain and cold like this one.
text.B2: The light down the street shows itself again. It shows where everyone swears blind that no one would be tonight. But a light means a hand to hold it up. And a hand means a person. A person out there, quite alone, in rain and cold like this — and you can't un-know that now.

text.A2: Now comes the long haul. You tend the pots, keep Gran Ivy warm upstairs, and watch the clock creep on. It's not exciting — just steady, careful, tiring work. But it's the whole job tonight. And it's yours.
text.B1: Now comes the long haul. You tend the pots, keep Gran Ivy warm upstairs, and watch the clock creep slowly on. It's not exciting — just steady, careful, tiring work. But it's the whole job tonight. And it's yours to do.
text.B2: Now comes the long haul of it. You tend the pots, keep Gran Ivy warm upstairs, and watch the clock creep slowly on toward seven. It isn't exciting work — just steady, careful, tiring work that nobody sees. But it's the whole job tonight, start to finish. And it's yours, and no one else's.

text.A2: And then, at last, it turns. The pots are nearly done. The table's set, the bread's warm, the smells fill the house. It's almost seven. You've nearly pulled the whole evening through.
text.B1: And then, at last, it turns. The pots are nearly done. The table's set, the bread's warm, and the smells fill the whole house. It's almost seven now. You've nearly pulled the whole evening through.
text.B2: And then, at long last, it turns. The pots are nearly done. The table's set, the bread's warm from the oven, and the good smells fill the whole house from top to bottom. It's almost seven now, almost time. You've very nearly pulled the whole long evening through on your own.

text.A2: This is the hardest stretch, the last one before it's done. Nothing's ready yet. Your arms ache, your eyes burn. But you can feel it all coming together, somewhere under the rush. Hold on a little longer.
text.B1: This is the hardest stretch, the last one before it's all done. Nothing's quite ready yet. Your arms ache, and your eyes burn. But you can feel it all coming together, somewhere under the rush. Hold on a little longer now.
text.B2: This is the hardest stretch of the whole night, the last one before it's finally done. Nothing's quite ready yet, not really. Your arms ache, and your eyes burn with tiredness. But you can feel it all starting to come together, somewhere under the rush and the noise. Just hold on a little longer now.

text.A2: You look out at the street. Warm windows glow all down the row. Other kitchens lit, other families, other dinners cooking in the rain. The whole street got through tonight too. You were never quite as alone as you felt.
text.B1: You look out at the street. Warm windows glow all the way down the row. Other kitchens lit, other families, other dinners cooking in the rain. The whole street got through this night too. You were never quite as alone as you'd felt.
text.B2: You look out at the dark street. Warm windows glow all the way down the row, one after another. Other kitchens lit, other families, other dinners cooking away in the rain. The whole street got through this night as well as you did. You were never, it turns out, quite as alone out here as you'd felt.

text.A2: At last, help comes through the door. The family, early, coats dripping — more hands, and quick ones. You lean on the counter and watch them pile in, your legs shaking under you now. But the worst of the night is behind you.
text.B1: At last, help comes through the door. The family, early, coats dripping — more hands, and quick ones at that. You lean on the counter and watch them pile in, your legs shaking under you now. But the worst of the night is behind you.
text.B2: At last, help comes through the door. The family, early, their coats dripping on the mat — more hands, and quick ones at that. text.A2: Too much came home at once.
text.B1: Too much came home at once.
text.B2: Too much came home at once.

text.A2: Seven o'clock comes round. The doorbell goes, and the family spill in out of the rain. The table is set, the food is hot, the house is warm. The worst has passed at last. You made it to the hour.
text.B1: Seven o'clock comes round. The doorbell goes, and the family spill in out of the rain. The table is set, the food is hot, and the house is warm. The worst has passed at last. You made it to the hour.

text.A2: Then it comes — a laugh from the front room, the first of the night. It rings through the house as if there'd been no rush at all. After the evening you've had, it seems almost absurd. And it's lovely, and you stop to listen.
text.B1: Then it comes — a laugh from the front room, the first real one of the night. It rings through the house as if there'd been no rush at all. After the evening you've had, it seems almost absurd. And it's lovely, and you stop just to listen.
text.B2: Then it comes — a laugh from the front room, the first real one of the whole night. It rings out through the house as if there'd never been any rush at all. After the evening you've just had, it seems almost absurd that such a sound could exist. And it's lovely, utterly lovely, and you stop whatever you're doing just to listen.

text.A2: From the window you watch the street. Lights come bobbing along, still too far to make out. Something is coming at last. But a light means someone out there. And someone is far better than no one tonight.
text.B1: From the window you watch the street. Lights come bobbing along it, still too far off to make out. Something is coming at last. But a light means someone out there. And someone is far better than no one tonight.
text.B2: From the window you watch the dark street below. Lights come bobbing along it, still too far off to make out properly. Something is coming at last, down there in the rain. But a light means someone out there, moving. And someone, on a night like this one, is far, far better than no one at all.

text.A2: Seven o'clock, and the evening adds up to what it is. Whatever you did out there in the rain comes home to you now. Some of it to be proud of, some not. Let's see, then, what it all came to.
text.B1: Seven o'clock, and the evening adds up to what it is. Whatever you did out there in the rain comes home to you now. Some of it to be proud of, some of it not. Let's see, then, what it all came to.
text.B2: Seven o'clock, and the evening adds up to just exactly what it is. Whatever you did out there in the cold and the rain comes home to you now, all of it. Some of it to be proud of, and some of it not so much. Let's see, then, what the whole long night finally came to in the end.

text.A2: The evening adds up — not with one big act, but with many small ones. What you cooked, what you refused, who you went out into the rain for. It all counts in the end. It all made the night what it was.
text.B1: The evening adds up — not with one big act, but with many small ones. What you cooked, what you refused, and who you went out into the rain for. It all counts in the end. It all made the night what it was.
text.B2: The evening adds up — not, in the end, with one big brave act, but with a great many small ones. What you cooked, what you refused to do, and who you went out into the cold rain for. It all counts in the end, every bit of it. It all made the night into exactly what it was.

text.A2: There's more to weigh; the night held other things too. A stranger you stopped for in the rain. Food off your own table, given with an open hand. Small choices, made in the cold, when it would have been easier not to.
text.B1: There's more to weigh; the night held other things too. A stranger you stopped for out in the rain. Food off your own table, given away with an open hand. Small choices, made in the cold, when it would have been far easier not to.
text.B2: There's more still to weigh up; the night held other things too, quieter ones. A stranger you stopped for out in the rain. Food off your own table, given away freely with an open hand. Small choices, all of them, made out in the cold, when it would have been so much easier simply not to bother.

text.A2: And what does the night leave you with? Maybe not a perfect dinner. Maybe just the fact that you tried, that you kept going. When it was late and cold and easy to give up, you didn't. That counts for something.
text.B1: And what does the night leave you with? Maybe not a perfect dinner. Maybe just the fact that you tried, and that you kept going. When it was late and cold and easy to give up, you didn't. That counts for something.

When it was late and cold and so easy to give the whole thing up, you simply didn't. And that, whatever else, counts for something.

text.A2: But not every night ends well. Some choices cost more than you knew at the time. Some things, once done, can't be undone. This is the hard end of the evening, where the worst of it comes home.

text.A2: You got the dinner made. By seven the table is full — hot food, warm bread, every chair taken. Gran Ivy comes down slow, on your arm, to a room full of her family. It all came good because you kept going and would not give up. That is the whole of it.

It all came good, every bit of it, because you kept going when you were soaked and worn out and would not let yourself give up. That, in the end, is the whole of it.

text.A2: You answered the light no one could explain. You found Nora out in the rain, lost and freezing. You got her in and warm just in time. And more than one thing was saved tonight. At the table, Gran Ivy looks up — and sees the granddaughter she lost years ago. A door everyone thought shut swings open again.

And more than one thing was saved tonight, as it turns out. At the table, Gran Ivy looks up — and sees the granddaughter she lost years ago, standing in her kitchen. A door everyone had thought shut for good swings quietly open again, and the dinner becomes something far bigger than a meal.

text.A2: There was no clever trick — there was something better. You turned a quiet, tired street into a kitchen full of people. Neighbours peeling, friends stirring, kids laying the table. Together you brought the whole evening through. No one sat alone tonight, and the house has not felt so full in years.

Together you brought the whole evening through. No one sat alone tonight, and the house hasn't felt so full in years.

Neighbours peeling, friends stirring the pots, kids squabbling over who lays the table. Together, all of you, you brought the whole evening through. No one sat alone tonight, not one soul, and the old house has not felt this full in years.

text.A2: You refused the con — saw Dale's trick for what it was and turned your back on it. You kept your head, and got the dinner on the table by honest work. It wasn't a perfect evening. You burned the odd thing and ran it close. But all of it was yours, and real, and that's worth more than any shortcut.

But every last bit of it was yours, and real, and that is worth a great deal more than any shortcut he was ever selling.

text.A2: You fell short of doing it all alone. But the stranger you stopped for earlier comes back now. They're at the door, a dish warm in their hands. They help you finish the dinner and warm the house. It's not the perfect evening. But a kindness, it turns out, has a way of coming back round.
text.B1: You fell short of doing it all on your own. But the stranger you stopped for earlier comes back now, at the door, with a dish in their hands. They help you finish the dinner and warm the house. It's not quite the perfect evening. But a kindness, it turns out, has a way of coming back round.
text.B2: You fell short of doing it all on your own, in the end. But the stranger you stopped for earlier comes back now, knocking at the door, with a covered dish warm in their hands. They stay, and help you finish the dinner and warm the house through. It's not quite the perfect evening you'd pictured. But a kindness, it turns out, has a quiet way of coming back round to you when you least expect it.

text.A2: You gave your own food away to those with less. So your table is plainer tonight — bread and soup, not the feast you planned. You didn't manage everything. But no one you met tonight goes to bed hungry. And somehow, shared out, there was always just about enough.

You didn't manage everything you set out to do. But no one you met out there tonight goes to bed hungry. And somehow, shared out between all those hands, there turned out to be always just about enough to go round.

text.A2: You scrape through the worst of it. The dinner's late, and a bit rough round the edges. But it lands on the table in the end. It's no triumph, and no one will tell stories about it. But the family ate, and laughed, and stayed warm. You got through the night, and that'll do.

You got through the night in one piece, and tonight, that will do nicely.

text.A2: You didn't pull off all you wanted. But the people round that table saw you try. They saw you come home soaked, and cook, and keep going when you could have stopped. They won't forget it. From tonight, you're the one who tried your heart out for them. And that stays.

From tonight on, you're the one who tried your heart out for them, on the worst of nights. And that, whatever else, stays with people.

text.A2: You took Dale's deal, and at the table it all comes out. Someone tastes it, frowns, and asks where it's really from. The lie unravels, dish by dish. The money's gone, the food's cold, and the evening dies in an awkward hush. You won't forget the look on Gran's face in a hurry.

You won't forget the look on Gran's face tonight in a hurry — nor, you suspect, will she.

text.A2: The main road was a trap, just as Joan warned. A car came too fast in the rain, and only a hard fall onto the kerb saved you. You limp home, soaked, shaken and hours too late. The family have long since gone. You should have gone the long way round, and you know it now.

text.B2: The main road was a trap, just exactly as Joan had warned you it would be. A car came too fast out of the rain, and only a hard, jarring fall back onto the kerb saved you at the very last second. You limp home after that, soaked, shaken, and hours too late for any of it. The family have long since given up and gone. You should have gone the long way round, like she said, and you know it now, too late.
